Every one of the **160 tools** carries a posture, and every call is judged against it before it runs. This page is generated from the configuration itself rather than described, because a description of it kept being wrong.

> These are the **shipped defaults**. What you can change lives in a
> config file you own once TESSERACT is installed, so your copy may
> differ, and should, once you tune it.

## What runs without asking

The remaining **120** run automatically. Most are reads — searching memory, listing a directory, looking something up. Some are not, and those are the ones worth knowing about: sending on a channel you connected, searching the web, writing to the assistant's own memory. Setting those up was the decision; being asked again each time would be noise.

## Two things that surprise people

**Read-only commands do not prompt.** 10 command patterns — running the tests, asking git what changed — are allowed in every mode. A prompt for `git status` is noise, and noise is what teaches people to click through prompts without reading them.

**There is more than one mode.** The shipped default is `max`, and there are 2 in total. The other is `free`, for unattended work: the assistant acts without asking, apart from a short list of tools named as still asking. It is not the default and turning it on is a deliberate act. It cannot reach a tool set to `deny` or the path rules below. It reaches one thing in the shell check list: the one-liner check, which asks in the default mode and runs unasked here, because a prompt nobody is there to answer is a refusal on a timer. The rest of that list is refused outright in this mode rather than asked, for the same reason.

## Paths beat tools

A tool's posture is not the last word. Path rules apply on top, and they can refuse what the tool alone would allow — the assistant cannot write to its own permissions file, to the runtime's source, or to `.env`, whatever `file_write` says. See `config/permissions.yaml` for the full list; it ships with the app.
